title: One More Each Time
keyIdea: Each counting number is one more than the number before it. Add one thing to a group of 5 and there are 6; add one more and there are 7. So one more than a number is the next number we say when we count, and one less is the number just before. You do not need to count a group again from 1: keep the number in your head and count on one.

kid: Here are 5 blocks. Put one more on top. Now there are 6. Put on one more. Now there are 7. Each time you add one, you get the next number.
So one more than 5 is 6. That is the number you say next when you count: 5, 6. One more than 9 is 10.
One less is the other way. Take one block off 7, and 6 are left. One less is the number you say just before.
If you know there are 6 in a box and one more goes in, you do not have to count them all again. Say 6 in your head, then say 7.
adult: This is the successor idea: each number in the counting sequence names a quantity exactly one larger than the number before it. The US Common Core puts it in Kindergarten (K.CC.4c, 'each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger'), and the English national curriculum asks Year 1 pupils, 'given a number, identify one more and one less'. Reception children meet it in the early learning goal for number.

It joins two skills your child may already have: saying the number names in order (the stable order) and knowing that the last number counted tells how many (cardinality). One more links them: moving one step along the count adds exactly one object. Counting on from a known number, instead of recounting from 1, grows out of this and leads to adding.

Common mistakes to watch for: saying the same number back (one more than 4 is 4); giving the number before (one more than 4 is 3); jumping two (4, then 6); and tipping out a group to count it all again from 1 when one more is added. Crossing a decade boundary is a classic slip too: one more than 9 is 10, and one more than 19 is 20, not 'ten-teen'.

In the lab your child drags cubes onto a tower and hears the next number each time, builds a staircase where each step is one cube taller, hops a frog one more along a 1 to 10 track, takes a cube away to find one less, and counts on from a number hidden in a cup.

familyTip: On the stairs, say the number of each step as you climb: one, two, three. Stop and ask, 'What number is one more step?' Then come down one and ask, 'What is one less?' At snack time, put 5 grapes in a cup, show one more going in, and ask how many without tipping them out.

visual.caption: 5 and one more. Push the groups together and count: there are 6.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: add one cube at a time, build a number staircase, hop one more on a track, take one away, and count on from a hidden number.

practice.prompt: Sam has {a} blocks. He adds one more. How many blocks now?
practice.hint: Say {a}, then say the next number.
practice.explain: One more than {a} is {=a+1}. It is the next number when we count.

practice.prompt: There are {a} birds on a wall. One flies away. How many are left?
practice.hint: One less is the number you say just before {a}.
practice.explain: One less than {a} is {=a-1}. It comes just before {a} when we count.

practice.hint: Count to 9. What number do you say next?
practice.explain: One more than 9 is 10. After 9 we say 10.

practice.prompt: There are 6 toys in a box. Mum puts in one more. What is the quick way to know how many?
choices: Tip them out and count from 1
practice.hint: You already know there are 6. Do you need to count those again?
practice.explain: Keep 6 in your head and count on one: 7. There are 7 toys.

pool.prompt: A tower has {a} cubes. You put one more on top. How many cubes now?
pool.hint: Adding one cube gives the next counting number after {a}.

pool.prompt: What number is one less than {a}?
pool.explain: One less than {a} is {=a-1}, the number just before it.

pool.prompt: Mia says one more than 4 is 3. Is she right?
pool.hint: One more makes the group bigger. Is 3 bigger than 4?
pool.explain: No. 3 is one less than 4. One more than 4 is 5, the number after it.

pool.hint: Count 5, 6, 7, and say the next one.
pool.explain: 8 comes just after 7, so 8 is one more than 7.

pool.prompt: Jo has 3 stickers. Kit has one more than Jo. How many does Kit have?
pool.hint: Start at 3 and count on just one.
pool.explain: One more than 3 is 4, so Kit has 4 stickers.

pool.prompt: A staircase has 1 block, then 2, then 3. How many blocks does the next step need?
pool.hint: Each step is one block taller than the step before.
pool.explain: Each step is one more. One more than 3 is 4, so the next step needs 4 blocks.

pool.prompt: Ben has 5 grapes. He eats one. Which is right?
pool.hint: Eating one makes the group smaller. Count back one.
pool.explain: Eating one takes one away. One less than 5 is 4.

pool.prompt: 8 ducks are on a pond. One more lands. How many now?
pool.hint: Say 8 in your head and count on one.
pool.explain: 8 and one more makes 9. 10 would be two more.
